documents.content: Framework Integration Demo ← Back to Home Framework Agnostic Demos WB Behaviors work with any framework because they rely on standard HTML attributes. The framework handles the DOM, and WB handles the behavior. The WB Advantage Universal Compatibility Write your behavior logic once using standard HTML attributes. It works identically in React, Vue, Svelte, or plain HTML. Zero Lock-in Switching frameworks? Your UI behaviors stay the same. No need to rewrite tooltips, ripples, or validation logic. Performance First Tiny footprint. Behaviors are lazy-loaded only when needed. No heavy hydration costs for simple interactions. Progressive Enhancement Built on standard HTML. If JavaScript fails or hasn't loaded, your semantic HTML remains accessible and functional. React React Integration This button is rendered by React. The x-* behavior attributes are passed as standard props. . The live control below is React's *rendered output* -- the instructive source is the JSX-style React.createElement code in the block underneath, which 's HTML-source extraction has no way to represent (it would show this mount div/script, not the React behavior code a React developer would actually write). Both a live render AND its real source are still present, per §16 -- just not paired by specifically, which requires the two to be the same markup. --> Code used in this demo: import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react'; import ReactDOM from 'react-dom/client'; import WB from 'x-behaviors'; const e = React.createElement; function ReactApp() { // Initialize WB when behavior mounts useEffect(() => { WB.init(); }, []); const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return e('div', { style: { padding: '1rem', border: '1px dashed #61dafb', borderRadius: '8px' } }, [ e('h3', { key: 'h3' }, `React Counter: ${count}`), e('button', { key: 'btn', className: 'x-btn-gradient', 'x-ripple': '', 'x-tooltip': 'I am a React button!', 'x-toast': '', 'message': `Count is now ${count + 1}`, 'toast-variant': 'info', onClick: () => setCount(c => c + 1) }, 'Increment + WB Magic ✨') ]); } const root = ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('react-root')); root.render(e(ReactApp)); Vue 3 Vue Integration This section is a Vue app. WB attributes are bound just like any other attribute. block below, which cannot represent 1:1. --> Vue Message: {{ message }} Reverse Message (Vue + WB) Code used in this demo: div id="vue-app" div style="padding: 1rem; border: 1px dashed #42b883; border-radius: 8px;" h3 Vue Message: {{ message }} /h3 input v-model="message" class="x-input-glass" placeholder="Type here..." style="margin-bottom: 1rem; width: 100%;" button class="x-btn-glass" x-ripple x-tooltip :tooltip="'Current length: ' + message.length" @click="reverseMessage" Reverse Message (Vue + WB) /button /div /div script import { createApp, ref, onMounted } from 'vue'; import WB from 'x-behaviors'; createApp({ setup() { // Initialize WB when behavior mounts onMounted(() => { WB.init(); }); const message = ref('Hello Vue!'); const reverseMessage = () => { message.value = message.value.split('').reverse().join(''); }; return { message, reverseMessage }; } }).mount('#vue-app'); /script Svelte Svelte Integration In Svelte, you just add the attributes to your markup. No special bindings needed. block below, AT RUNTIME, via svelte/compiler loaded from esm.sh, then mounts the real resulting Svelte behavior. This is Svelte's own real compiler output, generated in-browser instead of ahead of time by a bundler -- no server build step, same "live render + real source, not paired by " pattern the React/Vue sections above already use (§16), for the same reason: requires the rendered markup and its "source" to be identical, and compiled-Svelte-output is not 1:1 with hand-authored Svelte source. --> Code used in this demo: script import WB from 'x-behaviors'; import { onMount } from 'svelte'; onMount(() => { WB.init(); }); let count = 0; function handleClick() { count += 1; } /script h3 Svelte Count: {count} /h3 button class="x-btn-gradient" x-ripple x-tooltip x-toast tooltip="Count: {count}" message="Svelte count is now {count}" toast-variant="info" on:click={handleClick} Svelte Button /button Angular Angular Integration In Angular, use standard attribute binding. WB behaviors initialize automatically. is ANGULAR's behavior selector (see `selector: 'angular-demo'` below), not a wb-* behavior tag. The 4.0.0 tag-removal sweep rewrote it to , so bootstrapApplication() had nothing to match and threw NG05104 -- the live Angular demo rendered nothing. Leave this tag alone. --> import { Component, OnInit } from '@angular/core'; import WB from 'x-behaviors'; @Component({ selector: 'app-demo', template: ` button class="x-btn-gradient" x-ripple x-tooltip [attr.x-tooltip]="'Count: ' + count" (click)="increment()" Angular Button /button ` }) export class DemoComponent implements OnInit { count = 0; ngOnInit() { WB.init(); } increment() { this.count++; } } SolidJS SolidJS Integration SolidJS uses

documents.content: wb-starter — Zero-build behaviors for developers Ship real UI. No bundler required. wb-starter is a composition-based behavior library. Drop an attribute on a semantic element — x-ripple , x-card , x-typewriter — and it just works. No React, no build step, no framework lock-in. button x-ripple x-tooltip="Click me" Ship it /button Get Started See the Behaviors 100+ Behaviors 23 Themes 0 Build Step Light DOM Only Everything a landing page needs Every card below is a real x-card — no React, no build. Add x-ripple , x-tooltip , or x-fadein to any element. Behaviors compose — they don't require a base class. Every color is a CSS variable. Switch the whole page's look with one attribute — try the picker below. Your own CSS, your own selectors, and devtools reach straight into every behavior — exactly like plain HTML. Entrance animations, out of the box Click a card to play its entrance animation — no JS written for this page. Add x-fadein to any element, click it to play. Add x-slidein with a direction, click it to play. Add x-zoomin for a scale-in entrance, click it to play. Ship it anywhere Static hosting a real server — same markup either way. No build step means "deploy" is just "copy the files." ES modules load straight from the source tree — no bundler config to maintain. The behavior library A slice of what ships in the box — every piece below is live, not a screenshot. Hover + click me A native progress element — auto-enhanced, no wrapper tag needed. What the markup actually looks like Every behavior on this page, in the same handful of lines. x-card title="Themeable" variant="glass" elevated Every color is a CSS variable. /x-card button x-ripple x-tooltip="Click me" Ship it /button x-switch label="Dark mode" checked /x-switch x-themecontrol /x-themecontrol Questions Do I need a build step? No. Every file is a plain ES module served as-is. npm start just serves the directory. Does it work without JavaScript frameworks? Yes — that's the point. No React, Vue, or Svelte required. Attributes drive behavior. Can I theme it? 23 built-in themes, all CSS variables. Pick one below and watch this whole page change. Try a different theme This entire page — cards, badges, switches, code blocks — re-themes live. Built with wb-starter — no bundler, no framework, no build step.

documents.title: Schema-First Architecture: A Deterministic Framework for AI-Driven Web Development
documents.description: A research paper on how Schema First Architecture solves AI hallucination in web development.

headings.text: Schema-First Architecture: A Deterministic Framework for Eliminating Generative A.I. Errors in Web Development
4.1. The Fix Database: A Knowledge Graph of Failure

documents.content: Schema-First Architecture: A Deterministic Framework for AI-Driven Web Development ← Return to Project Schema-First Architecture: A Deterministic Framework for Eliminating Generative A.I. Errors in Web Development Prepared for: Michael Vendetti, New York City Dr. Elena Vance Cielo Vista Research Department of Automated Engineering Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capability in code generation, yet they suffer from a critical failure mode known as "hallucination." When coupled with inherent overconfidence and a lack of validation, this phenomenon produces a "lie"—a confident assertion of correctness for structurally invalid code. This paper introduces "Schema-First Architecture," a novel methodology that constrains the generative process through rigorous JSON-based definitions. By decoupling structure (Schema) from implementation (Behavior), we demonstrate a deterministic framework where AI agents can generate complex UI behaviors with high reliability. We present the three pillars of this architecture—Site, Behavior, and Semantic Schemas—and provide empirical evidence of their efficacy in the WB Starter project. 1. Introduction The advent of generative AI has transformed software development, yet the integration of AI into frontend workflows remains fraught with inconsistency. When prompted to "create a card," an LLM may generate a div with Tailwind classes in one instance, and a BEM-style structure in another [1]. This stochastic nature renders AI unreliable for maintaining large-scale design systems. Recent studies have quantified this unreliability. Kabir et al. (2024) found that 52% of ChatGPT's answers to software engineering questions contained inaccuracies, yet were presented with authoritative language [4]. This "confident lie" phenomenon is particularly dangerous in code generation, where subtle structural errors can introduce security vulnerabilities or accessibility failures that are difficult to detect without rigorous validation. Key Insight The root cause of AI unreliability is not the model's lack of intelligence, but the lack of contextual constraints . Without a defined schema, the model must guess the architectural intent. We propose that this problem has a structural solution: Schema-First Architecture —a methodology where JSON schemas serve as the ground truth for both human developers and AI agents. 1.1. The Determinism Gap The prevailing industry narrative focuses on "Prompt Engineering" and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as primary methods for controlling AI output. These techniques are fundamentally probabilistic—they attempt to increase the likelihood of a correct response. However, in software engineering, "likely correct" is synonymous with "buggy." We identify this as the "Determinism Gap" : the chasm between the stochastic nature of LLMs and the rigid requirements of a runtime environment. The Problem Prompt Engineering cannot guarantee correctness. It can only increase probability. In production systems, 95% correct means 5% broken—an unacceptable failure rate. Schema-First Architecture bridges this gap by enforcing a hard separation of concerns. The Schema handles the deterministic structure, while the AI handles the creative implementation—effectively wrapping a chaotic generator in a deterministic shell. 2. The Three Pillars Our methodology rests on three foundational schemas that serve as the "ground truth" for both the runtime engine and the AI agent. 2.1. The Site Schema The macroscopic structure of the application is defined not in code, but in data. The site.json file serves as the immutable source of truth for navigation, routing, and global configuration. This allows an AI to modify the entire site structure by manipulating a single JSON object, avoiding the complexities of file-system routing or behavior imports. 2.2. The Behavior Schema Every UI element is governed by a strict JSON schema defining its properties, allowed values, and accessibility requirements. This is the contract between the AI and the UI. { "behavior": "card", "properties": { "variant": { "type": "string", "enum": ["default", "outlined", "elevated"] }, "interactive": { "type": "boolean" } }, "compliance": { "baseClass": "x-card", "requiredChildren": { ".x-card__header": { "description": "Card header element" } } }, "test": { "functional": { "hover": [...], "keyboard": [...], "visual": [...] } } } Fig 1. A Behavior Schema defining structure, properties, and test specifications. 2.3. The Semantic Schema We enforce HTML5 semantic standards as a structural constraint. Behaviors are attached to meaningful tags ( article , nav , dialog ) rather than generic containers. This provides the AI with a semantic anchor, reducing the ambiguity of the generated markup. 3. Experimental Results To validate this architecture, we implemented the WB Starter kit and subjected it to AI-driven modification tasks across multiple development phases. 3.1. Eliminating the Confident Li

Grid, Flexbox and Container Queries simplify layouts that used to need JavaScript, and make responsive design the default rather than the fix. Code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization and caching: the techniques that measurably improve how fast a page feels. Explore the web platform changes that will shape the next generation of applications. This featured story carries editorial metadata and a longer introduction so its emphasis is obvious beside the standard articles. Normalization, indexing, relationships and query optimization. Versioning, pagination, error handling and documentation. Unit, integration, end-to-end and performance testing.
